solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Spill drops on small dish (8)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a platter is a large serving dish

annotation.surface: Someone clumsy lets drops fall onto a little dish.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spill drops' reads as noun and verb in the surface, but together they are the verb phrase: to splatter is to spill drops about.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: paint or gravy flung about in drops has been splattered.

entries.clue: Old hat worn by one very reluctant to get involved (7)

indicatorNotes.worn by: a hat is worn around a head, so PASSE goes around the letters

blocks.note: old hat = passé, out of date

annotation.surface: An old hat is worn by someone who just won't join in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old hat' looks like headgear but is the idiom for outdated; 'worn by' then fits it round I and V.
annotation.definitionFit: A passive person holds back and does not get involved.

entries.clue: In shop ordered to follow a group safety directive (7,4)

indicatorNotes.ordered: put in a new order, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.to follow: the rearranged letters come after A BAND

blocks.note: a band is a group of musicians
the six letters of IN SHOP rearranged

annotation.surface: A shopkeeper orders staff to line up behind a group for a fire drill.
annotation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder comes first in the clue but last in the answer; 'to follow' is what tells you to put it after A BAND.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Abandon ship!' is the order given to save lives when a vessel is sinking.

entries.clue: Not very good time to put up several patrols (5)

indicatorNotes.to put up: in a down entry, putting up means writing the letters bottom to top

annotation.surface: A sergeant grumbles that it is a bad moment to send out more patrols.
annotation.walkthrough: A scout troop is divided into small groups called patrols, so a troop is several patrols.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by structure: Scout units are split into small patrols, and several patrols together form the larger unit.

entries.clue: Transport old phones (not black) and have half disconnected (7)

indicatorNotes.not: B (black) is not to be kept, so it is removed
indicatorNotes.half disconnected: half of the word is cut off, leaving only its first half

blocks.note: BRICKS, slang for the chunky early mobile phones, minus B = black

annotation.surface: Old telephones are cut off and half of what you have goes with them.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Phones' and 'disconnected' paint a telecoms picture; the answer is a man-pulled cart, in a less common spelling of rickshaw.
annotation.definitionFit: A ricksha (rickshaw) is a light two-wheeled vehicle pulled by a person.

entries.clue: Exactly what remains when husband and wife leave show? (4,2)

indicatorNotes.leave: H and W depart from the word, so they are removed

blocks.note: a word meaning 'only', describing how little of SHOW is left

blocks.clueFragment: when husband and wife leave show

annotation.surface: A couple walk out of a show, and we wonder what is left.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes its answer: take H and W from SHOW and you are left with 'just SO'.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Just so' means exactly, precisely right.

entries.clue: Perhaps one unemployed comedian keeps bees for a change (9)

indicatorNotes.keeps: JOKER holds the other letters inside it
indicatorNotes.for a change: the letters of BEES are changed round

annotation.surface: A comedian with no gigs takes up beekeeping as a new line of work.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' signals that a jobseeker is one example of an unemployed person.
annotation.definitionFit: A jobseeker is someone out of work and looking for a job.

entries.clue: Object of pagan worship endlessly hymned (3)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: without its end, so the last letter goes

annotation.surface: Pagans sing endless hymns to the thing they worship.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hymned' is a past participle, sung, and cutting its end leaves the object many ancient religions worshipped.
annotation.definitionFit: The sun was worshipped as a god by many pagan cultures.

entries.clue: Immigrant in centre of village I must welcome (7)

indicatorNotes.centre of: take the middle letter of the word
indicatorNotes.must welcome: to welcome is to take in, so SETTER goes around L

blocks.note: in a crossword, 'I' is the setter speaking

annotation.surface: A villager insists on welcoming a newcomer to the heart of the village.
annotation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'I' as the letter; setters often use it for themselves, giving SETTER.
annotation.definitionFit: A settler is someone who moves to live in a new country or region.

entries.clue: Powerless committee members dog can bite badly (6,7)

indicatorNotes.badly: the letters are put together wrongly, so rearranged

blocks.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely, to shadow

annotation.surface: A dog savages some members of a committee who can do nothing about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Dog' is a verb here. In Britain the shadow cabinet is the opposition's team of would-be ministers, who hold no power.
annotation.definitionFit: The shadow cabinet is the opposition's senior team, mirroring government ministers without power.

entries.clue: Frightened people may get this bit of teasing (4-2)

blocks.note: British idiom: the scared are said to get 'the ___ ___', a nervous gust
British slang for a joke played to provoke someone, from winding a person up like a clock spring

annotation.surface: Nervous people are the easiest targets for a bit of teasing.
annotation.walkthrough: Both senses are British idiom: frightened people 'get the wind up', and a wind-up is a tease.
annotation.definitionFit: A wind-up is a prank to provoke someone; 'the wind up' is what the scared get.

entries.clue: Small area with gardens, bare white with patches of colour (8)

blocks.note: Kew is a district of London home to the Royal Botanic Gardens

annotation.surface: A small, bare patch of land sits among white gardens with bits of colour.
annotation.walkthrough: Skewbald describes a horse with white and non-black patches; piebald is the black-and-white version.
annotation.definitionFit: A skewbald horse has patches of white and another colour, usually brown.

entries.clue: Tours having time off now as airline grounded over a year (8,3)

indicatorNotes.over: in a down entry, the airline sits over, above, what follows

annotation.surface: Tourists complain about delays as an airline's fleet is grounded for a year.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tours' is not trips but the French city: its people have 14 July off, and 'now' says the puzzle appeared around that date.
annotation.definitionFit: Bastille Day, 14 July, is France's national holiday, so the city of Tours takes the day off.

entries.clue: Coin, reverse impressed with large stamp (5,5)

indicatorNotes.impressed with: to be impressed with a mark is to have it pressed in, so L goes inside BACK

blocks.note: the reverse of a coin is its back

annotation.surface: A coin's reverse is struck with a big design, as a stamp would be.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reverse' looks like a reversal instruction but is the back of the coin; 'stamp' here is the postal kind.
annotation.definitionFit: The Penny Black of 1840 was the world's first adhesive postage stamp.

entries.clue: Drunken reveller returned to speak, obsessively controlling (9)

indicatorNotes.to speak: as the word is spoken, so a sound-alike spelling is used

blocks.note: returned = back; BACCH is said the same way
anal = fussily obsessed with order and control

annotation.surface: A drunk comes home to talk and turns into a control freak.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Returned' is not a reversal: it means BACK, which is then spelt as it sounds at the start of Bacchus, god of wine.
annotation.definitionFit: Named after Bacchus, Roman god of wine; his followers' riotous drinking gave the word for any boozy carouser.

entries.clue: Irrational and ridiculous, scrapping a book (4)

indicatorNotes.scrapping: throwing out, so A and B are dropped

annotation.surface: Someone calls it silly and pointless to throw out a book.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Irrational' is the maths sense: a surd is a root that cannot be written as a fraction, like the square root of 2.
annotation.definitionFit: A surd is an irrational number, such as the square root of 2.

entries.clue: Eat out and so on at hotel (4)

indicatorNotes.at: H is placed at the end, after ETC

blocks.note: etc = et cetera, and so on
H = hotel in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Dining out and similar things take place at a hotel.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Eat out' is not dining: acid eats out a design when it etches metal.
annotation.definitionFit: To etch is to eat away a surface with acid to make a design.

entries.clue: Adolescent drops seed, husked, for a songbird (7)

indicatorNotes.drops: lets go of letters, so EE comes out
indicatorNotes.husked: with its outer shell removed, so only the inner letters of SEED remain
indicatorNotes.for: in exchange for, so A replaces what was dropped

blocks.note: A goes in where EE came out

annotation.surface: A teenager scatters seed for a garden bird.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface feeds a bird, but 'for' is doing swap work: EE out of TEENAGER, A in.
annotation.definitionFit: Tanagers are brightly coloured American songbirds.

entries.clue: Policeman about to go into inner working of old scientist (10)

indicatorNotes.to go into: CA is put inside the other letters
indicatorNotes.working: the letters of INNER are worked into a new order

annotation.surface: A policeman is about to examine the inner workings of an old scientist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About to' is split: 'about' gives CA and 'to go into' puts it inside.
annotation.definitionFit: Copernican means relating to Copernicus, the 16th-century astronomer.

entries.clue: Worst and best places to break journey (3,4)

annotation.definitionNote: plural in the clue, singular answer: each pit stop is one such place
annotation.surface: A review of the worst and best stops along a road trip.
annotation.walkthrough: The join moves: the S ending 'the pits' slides across the word break, so the enumeration (3,4) does not match the parts.
annotation.definitionFit: A pit stop is a brief halt during a journey.

entries.clue: Narrow lanes keeping European extremely vigilant (3,4)

indicatorNotes.keeping: to keep something is to hold on to it, so the lanes hold the European within them

annotation.surface: A European walking narrow backstreets stays very alert.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' is part of the definition, not an instruction to take outer letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: someone so watchful they seem made of nothing but eyes is extremely vigilant.

entries.clue: Picture biscuits straight from the oven? (8)

blocks.note: fresh out of the oven = hot

annotation.surface: Someone photographs biscuits just out of the oven.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Biscuits' is British for cookies; ginger snaps are the ones meant.
annotation.definitionFit: A snapshot is a quick informal photograph.

entries.clue: Mostly drunk portrait painter is alone (6)

indicatorNotes.Mostly: most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

blocks.note: SOT, a drunk, without its last letter
Sir Peter Lely, court portrait painter to Charles II

annotation.surface: A portrait painter, half-cut, drinks by himself.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drunk' is a noun, a sot, not the adjective.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: done solely by her means done by her alone.

entries.clue: Picked up sections for binder (5)

indicatorNotes.Picked up: lifted, and in a down entry that means written bottom to top

annotation.surface: Pages are collected into sections for a ring binder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' wants to be a homophone signal; in a down entry it reverses.
annotation.definitionFit: A strap binds or fastens things together.

entries.clue: Ugly deodorant sprayed in amicable manner (4-9)

indicatorNotes.sprayed: scattered about, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: Someone sprays an unpleasant deodorant, and is pleasant about it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Ugly' looks like the opposite of the definition, which is what makes it good cover: it is only letters to be mixed.
annotation.definitionFit: Good-naturedly means in a kindly, friendly way.

entries.clue: I’m surprised, when told, to be in debt (3)

indicatorNotes.when told: said out, so the answer sounds like the word

annotation.surface: Someone is shocked to learn they are in debt.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation is the sound 'oh', which shares its pronunciation with a verb of borrowing.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: if you owe money you are in debt to the lender.

entries.clue: Creator of Big Brother’s fully behind men (6)

indicatorNotes.behind: to be behind is to come after, so this piece follows the men in the answer

blocks.note: OR = other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: The creator of Big Brother is right behind the men.
annotation.walkthrough: Big Brother here is the watchful ruler of Nineteen Eighty-Four, not the TV show.
annotation.definitionFit: George Orwell created Big Brother in Nineteen Eighty-Four.

entries.clue: Quietly snobby about Yankee resembling young boxer? (8)

indicatorNotes.about: about means around, so the snobby word wraps round the Yankee letter

blocks.note: Y = Yankee in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: A quiet snob sneers at an American who is like a young fighter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boxer' is the dog breed, and the question mark flags it; a young dog is a puppy.
annotation.definitionFit: Resembling a young boxer dog means being like a puppy.
